query: Single-phase high-entropy alloys have difficulty achieving a satisfactory strength–ductility balance. Earlier work introduced the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with a uniform, fine lamellar structure to enable large-sized production and obtain good strength and plasticity, but its performance still falls short of industrial requirements. Its use in aircraft and spacecraft fasteners further requires stability under extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading, room-temperature creep, and corrosion, while relevant creep and corrosion studies remain limited by sample-size and experimental-environment constraints. Given these limitations and design requirements, what single intervention could improve the alloy’s practical performance? Present one hypothesis that specifies the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted improvement over the starting material, boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a feasible experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a minor dopant of yttrium (Y) to the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy will improve its long-term stability (creep resistance), high‐temperature corrosion resistance, and tolerance to extreme temperature fluctuations without compromising its strength–ductility balance.
generation.material_initial_state: As‐cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high‐entropy alloy, exhibiting a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure that already shows a good strength and ductility balance but has issues with creep and corrosion under severe temperature and loading conditions.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled, minor alloying addition of yttrium (Y) into the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 composition during melting and casting.
generation.conditions: The Y-doped alloy will be produced with the same conventional casting and thermo-mechanical processing used for the baseline alloy. Subsequent evaluation will include high-temperature exposure (e.g., 900 °C in a molten salt environment of 75% Na2SO4 + 25% NaCl), room-temperature creep testing under long-term mechanical loading, and cyclic temperature fluctuation tests.
generation.structural_mediator: Yttrium preferentially segregates to grain boundaries and phase interfaces within the lamellar structure, potentially forming stable, fine yttrium-rich precipitates that pin boundaries and stabilize the microstructure against creep and high-temperature corrosion.
generation.mechanism: The presence of Y at the grain boundaries reduces atomic diffusion and grain boundary mobility (thereby limiting creep) and promotes the formation of protective oxide scales during high-temperature exposure. These effects enhance both mechanical stability under long-term loading and resistance to corrosive environments without degrading the alloy’s inherent strength and plasticity.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy, the Y-doped alloy is expected to show improved room-temperature creep resistance, a reduced extent of corrosion scale spallation under high-temperature corrosive conditions, and maintained (or only slightly altered) tensile strength and ductility.
generation.baseline: As-cast and processed AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy performance as previously reported, with good strength and ductility but limited data on long-term creep and high-temperature corrosion stability.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies under processing conditions similar to the baseline alloy. The optimal Y concentration must be low enough to avoid significant microstructural changes (e.g., coarsening of lamellae), and the benefits are expected provided that yttrium is uniformly distributed at critical interfaces.
generation.uncertainty: The ideal dopant level of Y and its effect on the fine lamellar microstructure are not yet established; excessive Y might induce undesired phase formation or microstructural coarsening.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of samples: one set of baseline AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA and one set with a minor (controlled) addition of Y. Process both sets under identical casting and thermo-mechanical conditions. Subject these samples to (i) high-temperature hot corrosion tests at 900 °C in a molten salt environment, (ii) long-term room-temperature creep tests under a fixed load, and (iii) cyclic temperature fluctuation tests to simulate aerospace conditions.
measurements: Grain boundary and interfacial stability (using electron microscopy and chemical analysis)
Room-temperature creep rate under a specified constant load
Extent of oxide scale spallation and corrosion area after hot corrosion tests
Tensile strength and elongation from mechanical testing
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Y-doped alloy does not show a statistically significant reduction in creep rate, improved corrosion resistance (e.g., reduced spallation area), or comparable tensile performance relative to the baseline alloy, then the hypothesis that Y addition enhances the alloy's practical performance is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractBoth crack-free AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) and Y and Hf co-doping AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA (YHf-EHEA) coatings were prepared by laser cladding. The solidification microstructure, thermal stability, and hot corrosion performance of the coatings at 900 °C under 75% Na2SO4 + 25% NaCl molten salts were investigated. The experimental results showed that the structure of the as-deposited coatings consisted of FCC and BCC/B2 phases. After heat treatment, an Al-rich L12 phase was precipitated in the FCC phase of all coatings. The grain sizes of the EHEA and YHf-EHEA coatings after heat treatment at 900 °C for 10 h increased by 27.5% and 15.7%, respectively, compared to the as-deposited coatings. Meanwhile, after hot corrosion, the spallation areas of the YHf-EHEA and EHEA coatings accounted for 14.98% and 5.67% of the total surface area, respectively.
